subject: Ottawa's budget picks tax breaks over AI grants
bodyMarkdown:
Canada's budget landed yesterday afternoon, and if you own shares in a private company or run one, a few lines in it change your math. The October jobs numbers come out at 8:30 this morning, so by lunch we will know whether the economy Ottawa just budgeted for is the one we have.

## The tax side is the real news

The headline measure is the Canada Growth Incentive, a capital gains exemption of up to $15 million on qualifying shares of qualifying corporations, and it applies to shares issued on or after November 5, 2026 and before 2037. The Globe and Mail compared it to a Silicon Valley incentive for entrepreneurs and investors, and that reads right: it tries to make funding a Canadian company pay off here rather than in Delaware. Next to it, the Productivity Mega Deduction lifts the write-off rate on Canadian development expense from 30 to 100 per cent. Finance says that pulls the **marginal effective tax rate**, the share of a new investment's return that tax takes, down from 13 per cent to 6.4 per cent, and that it now covers roughly two thirds of capital asset spending against about 15 per cent under last year's super-deduction. $930 million also extends SR&ED claims to some commercialization costs.

## The AI money is mostly old money

Ottawa says it wants Canadian AI firms to have access to 500 megawatts of sovereign compute, and it plans to get there using backstops and **offtake agreements**, contracts where government promises in advance to buy a share of what a facility produces so a private builder can finance it. The Globe and Mail reported Thursday that the budget carries little new AI funding and mostly books the $2.04 billion already pledged under the national AI strategy released in June. BetaKit counted $1 billion over five years for a Government Transformation Fund for government IT. The one genuinely large cheque came a week earlier, on October 29, when the Prime Minister's Office announced an equity investment of up to $1.6 billion in Cohere, staged, and conditioned on the company staying headquartered in Canada, at least $1.7 billion more in Canadian computing infrastructure by 2030, and 1,000 new technical jobs.

## Who carries it

I promised yesterday to take the borrowing plan apart, so: the deficit is $62.3 billion for 2026-27, CBC reported, down from the $65.3 billion projected in April, with $142 billion in new measures over five years. The Globe puts federal debt at $1.36 trillion this fiscal year, or 39.9 per cent of GDP. Debt service is the line I keep staring at, rising from $60.2 billion in 2026-27 to $85.5 billion by 2030-31 on CBC's numbers. That is a quarter again as much, and it buys nothing. **Gross issuance**, the total new bonds Ottawa floats in a year, steps up to $316 billion in FY27/28, which BMO called broadly in line with expectations, and the weight sits at the short end, roughly $120 billion of two-year paper against $24 billion of thirties. So Ottawa is not what moves the long end this month. The Parliamentary Budget Officer doubts the targets, and sees deficits cumulatively $44.7 billion larger over five years.

## The takeaway

Watch the Labour Force Survey at 8:30 this morning. Consensus sits at 6.5 per cent unemployment after September shed 68,300 jobs, mostly in education and health care, while RBC looks for a dip to 6.4 per cent. A soft print makes a budget this expansionary easier to defend, and a firm one hands the Bank of Canada, which raised its rate to 2.50 per cent on October 28 for the first time since July 2023, a reason to move again at its December 9 decision. If you hold shares in a private Canadian company, or are about to issue any, ask an accountant about that November 5 start date this week instead of next.
